analysis_notes.gap_analysis_detail: Torah 93 is not a formal Torah teaching — it is introduced with 'שָׁמַעְתִּי בִּשְׁמוֹ' (I heard in his name), indicating an oral tradition or brief reported remark rather than an elaborated teaching. Its entire content is a single explanatory statement: because the Rebbe's occupation was entirely with תְּפִלָּה (prayer) and הִתְבּוֹדְדוּת (personal prayer and meditation), people belittled him and disputed him (מַחֲלֹקֶת), and this is explained by the Talmudic dictum (Berakhot 6) — 'כְּרוּם זֻלֻּת לִבְנֵי אָדָם — אֵלּוּ דְּבָרִים הָעוֹמְדִים בְּרוּמוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם, וּבְנֵי אָדָם מְזַלְזְלִין בָּהֶם, וּמַאי נִיהוּ תְּפִלָּה' (When the vile are exalted — these are things that stand at the height of the world yet people treat them lightly, and what are they? Prayer). The text contains no bechina formulations of the Rebbe's own (no 'הוּא בְּחִינַת', 'נִקְרָא', or equivalent equivalence language). The implicit identification of תְּפִלָּה with 'דְּבָרִים הָעוֹמְדִים בְּרוּמוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם' is a direct Talmudic citation, not a new bechina introduced by the Rebbe. The causal logic of the text is eitza in nature: Rebbe engaged in prayer → prayer is what people despise (Talmud) → therefore people despised and disputed him. No bechina concepts are present in the source text that are absent from the dataset. The dataset correctly contains no edges for reference 1093.
